title: Edtech Wiggle Room, Private Equity Hack SPED, & More Layoffs
author: Alexander Russo
summary: Alexander Russo's weekly survey of education journalism leads with what he reads as the defining fault line of the moment: not whether schools should worry about technology, but whether the answer is a categorical ban or a more selective push toward software that actually works. He marshals polling and reports indicating that parents and teachers favor limits over prohibition, and points to an evaluation distinguishing general-purpose chatbots from targeted tools. He is careful to note that the action is bipartisan, with Florida joining the rule-setting states and NYC lawmakers now eyeing a YouTube ban, and he flags a press failure worth naming: coverage of the debate vastly outruns reporting on what is happening in classrooms. The curation section then awards three pieces, each with a short critical appraisal rather than a summary, praising The 74's private equity investigation for staying legible across 6,000 words and faulting The Assembly's retention piece for being compressed into one story when it could have been a series. A closing section tallies the shrinking education beat itself, with McClatchy and Gannett layoffs set against a handful of new hires. The issue is a media critic's ledger as much as a news digest.
points: Russo frames the week's dominant story as a widening split between school tech skeptics who want categorical bans and those pushing for effective software plus careful implementation.

He notes polling from Chalkbeat, the NYT, Gallup and NBC suggesting parents and teachers want limits rather than outright prohibition, and cites an evaluation finding general-purpose chatbots the biggest threat while targeted tools like Khanmigo and Quill fare best.

The issue's award picks are an investigation by The 74 into private equity capture of Medicaid-funded autism therapy, a Hechinger piece on private schools' lack of legal obligation to accommodate voucher students with disabilities, and The Assembly's data reporting on post-ninth-grade retention in North Carolina.
Russo faults the press for covering the policy debate far more than classroom reality, calling it an open opportunity for enterprising reporters.
The issue also tracks the contraction of the education beat itself, including McClatchy and Gannett layoffs alongside a thin trickle of new hires and open positions.
quotes: The big education news of the week is the growing split between those most concerned about tech in schools with those who want to hone in on effective learning software and mindful implementation rather than time limits or categorical bans.

According to one new evaluation, general-use chatbots pose the biggest threat to student learning, while targeted tools like Khanmigo and Quill produce “the most consistent and strongest learning experiences.
There’s much more coverage of the debate than of what’s actually going on in classrooms — a great opportunity for enterprising reporters.

Over the course of 6,000 words, the reporters explain the niceties of therapy techniques, insurance regulation, state legislation, and private equity. The fact that the story remains clear and easy to follow is a minor miracle.

It’s a well-balanced story, showing both how private schools sometimes can provide resources and opportunities that would be otherwise unavailable for students — but can also drop them in a way public schools cannot.
Elementary school retention gets most of the attention, but in North Carolina the spike in student retention occurs after 9th grade.
The story is an impressive piece of data reporting, even if it feels in places like it could have been a series.
NBC’s Tyler Kingkade has his finger on the pulse of the edtech beat in a way few other reporters do — so it was great to have him on for a conversation about the state of schools as of mid-September.
